blocks.text: The previous lesson explained why MCP needed to exist in broad, economic terms, too much repeated, inconsistent, custom integration work. This lesson gets specific: five distinct technical problems, each one genuinely hard to solve well without a shared protocol, and each one MCP addresses directly and deliberately.
1. The Discovery Problem

blocks.alt: An AI model is checked for whether it can discover tools

blocks.text: Before an AI model can use a tool, something has to know that tool exists and what it needs as input.
Without a standard, this "something" was almost always a human developer, reading documentation and hard-coding a specific tool’s existence into an application.

MCP solves this with a simple, mandatory discovery step, a client can ask any MCP server, "what tools, resources, and prompts do you offer," and get back a complete, structured answer, no advance human research required.

blocks.title: Why this matters more than it sounds
blocks.content: Discovery is what makes it possible for a brand-new server, one the client has literally never seen before, to be usable immediately, with zero code changes on the client side.

blocks.text: This also means new capabilities can be added to a server over time, and any connected client will automatically see them the next time it asks, no separate announcement or manual update required on the client side.

code.content:
# a client periodically re-checking for newly added tools
tools_before = set(t["name"] for t in client.list_tools())
# ... server gets updated with a new tool ...
tools_after = set(t["name"] for t in client.list_tools())
print(tools_after - tools_before)

blocks.text: 2. The Schema Consistency Problem

blocks.alt: Server A schema is compared against server B schema in the same format

blocks.text: Even when two different tools are discoverable, if one describes its inputs one way and another describes them a completely different way, an AI application still has to write custom parsing logic for each.

MCP fixes this by requiring every tool description to follow the same schema format, based on JSON Schema, a well-established standard for describing the shape of data, so that one piece of client code can correctly interpret any MCP server’s tool descriptions, not just ones it was specifically written for.

JSON Schema was a deliberate choice here rather than something invented from scratch, it is already a widely used, well-documented standard for describing data shapes, which means tooling and validation libraries already exist for it in nearly every programming language.

This also means AI models themselves, many of which were already trained on large amounts of JSON Schema found across the public internet, tend to interpret MCP tool schemas particularly well, since the format is not a bespoke invention unfamiliar to the model.
3. The Portability Problem

Tool integrations built directly against one AI model provider’s specific function-calling format do not automatically work with a different provider’s model. This locks a team into whichever model they originally built for, or forces a rewrite every time they want to switch. MCP sits underneath the model, as a separate layer, so the same MCP server keeps working no matter which MCP-compatible model or client ends up calling it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Without MCP","With MCP"],"rows":[["Tool code tied to one model’s function-call format","Tool code speaks MCP, independent of model choice"],["Switching models means rewriting integrations","Switching models means reconnecting the same servers"]]}

blocks.text: This portability also protects a team’s investment in the tool integrations themselves, the engineering effort spent building a good MCP server keeps paying off release after release, model after model, rather than becoming stranded the moment a team wants to try a different model.

It also protects against a subtler risk, a model provider changing or deprecating its own function-calling format over time, since the MCP layer in between absorbs that change without every downstream tool integration needing to be touched.
4. The Context-Sharing Problem

blocks.alt: A resource becomes shared context for the model

blocks.text: Tools are only half the picture, an AI model often also needs relevant background information, a file’s contents, a database record, a document, fed into its context window before it can reason well.
Before MCP, feeding this kind of live, external context into a model was handled ad hoc, different applications had different, incompatible ways of fetching and formatting it.
MCP’s resources concept, covered in full in its own module later in this curriculum, standardizes exactly this, giving external context a well-defined, discoverable, and readable shape.

Resources are deliberately kept separate from tools in the protocol, a resource is something to read, a tool is something to do, and keeping that distinction explicit helps both server authors and client authors reason clearly about what a given piece of functionality is actually for.

code.content:
# a resource is read, a tool is invoked, kept deliberately distinct
file_content = client.read_resource("file:///project/README.md")
result = client.call_tool("run_tests", {"path": "./tests"})

blocks.text: This separation also helps with performance, a client can choose to only fetch resources it actually needs for a given task, rather than every tool call implicitly dragging along unrelated context by default.
5. The Reusable Instruction Problem
" Before MCP, these templates lived scattered across different applications, in different formats, tightly coupled to whichever app built them.

MCP’s prompts concept lets a server expose these templates in a standard way, so any MCP client can list them, fill in their parameters, and use them, regardless of which application built the underlying server.

Because prompts can accept parameters, the same underlying template, "draft a bug report about {issue}," can be reused across many different specific situations, rather than needing a brand new, hard-coded template for every slightly different case.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Without prompts","With MCP prompts"],"rows":[["Templates hard-coded per application","Templates discoverable and reusable across clients"],["Updating a template means updating every app","Updating a template updates it everywhere at once"]]}

blocks.title: A useful distinction
blocks.content: A tool does something, a prompt suggests how to ask for something, keeping this line clear helps when deciding whether a new piece of functionality belongs in one bucket or the other.

blocks.text: 6. The Error Handling Problem

blocks.alt: A tool call follows a standardized error format

blocks.text: When a tool call fails, and it eventually always does, a network hiccup, an invalid argument, a downstream service being temporarily down, something needs to communicate that failure back to the model in a way it can actually understand and react to.
Without a shared format, every integration reported failure differently, sometimes silently.
MCP defines a standard error response shape, so a client, and by extension the model, always knows how to recognize and handle a failure, regardless of which server produced it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Failure type","What a standardized MCP error communicates"],"rows":[["Invalid arguments","Which input was invalid and why"],["Tool execution failure","That the tool ran but did not succeed"],["Server unavailable","That the connection itself is the problem, not the tool logic"]]}

code.content:
# a standardized error shape a client can always rely on
{"error": {"code": "invalid_arguments", "message": "city is required"}}

blocks.text: A model that receives this kind of clear, structured error can often recover gracefully on its own, for instance by asking the user a clarifying question, rather than the whole interaction simply failing silently or crashing.

Standardizing error shape also makes centralized logging and alerting dramatically simpler, a monitoring system can watch for the same error fields across every connected server, rather than needing custom parsing logic per integration.
7. The Session and State Problem

blocks.alt: A session lets state persist across calls

blocks.text: Some tool interactions are not one-shot, a model might need to open a file, read part of it, then read more, all as part of one coherent interaction with a server, rather than a series of unrelated calls.
Before MCP, managing this kind of ongoing, stateful interaction was handled inconsistently across applications.
MCP formalizes a session, an ongoing connection between one client and one server, with a well-defined lifecycle, covered fully in the Session Lifecycle lesson later in this module.

A well-defined session lifecycle also makes cleanup predictable, when a conversation ends, the client and server both know exactly how to close the connection cleanly, rather than leaving a resource-consuming connection open by accident.

blocks.title: A helpful mental model
blocks.content: Think of a session the same way you would think of a phone call, it has a clear beginning, an ongoing conversation in the middle, and a clear, deliberate end, rather than an undefined, ambiguous connection that just eventually stops.

blocks.text: A session boundary also gives both sides a clean, well-defined place to handle reconnection after a dropped network connection, discussed in more depth in the Reconnection Strategies lesson in the Transport Mechanisms module.
8. The Security Boundary Problem

blocks.alt: A client passes through a permission boundary to reach the server

blocks.text: Giving an AI model the power to take real actions is inherently risky if that power is not carefully scoped, an overly broad tool could delete data it should never have touched.

" MCP does not remove this responsibility, but it does give the whole ecosystem shared vocabulary and shared mechanisms, capabilities and permissions, covered in the Authentication & Security module, to build consistent, reviewable safeguards around.

blocks.title: An important nuance
blocks.content: MCP standardizes how permissions and capabilities are described and requested, it does not, by itself, decide which specific permissions any given deployment should grant, that judgment call still belongs to whoever configures the server.

blocks.text: Different servers naturally need different levels of caution too, a read-only weather lookup carries far less risk than a tool that can send money, and the same standardized permission vocabulary applies cleanly to both extremes.
9. The Multi-Tool Coordination Problem

blocks.alt: Tool A and tool B combine into a coordinated result

blocks.text: A realistic AI agent task often spans several tools working together, searching the web, then saving a summary to a document, then notifying a teammate.
Without a shared interface, coordinating three differently-shaped integrations inside one coherent agent loop was its own significant engineering challenge.
With MCP, every one of those three tools looks the same to the agent’s reasoning loop, discover, call, receive a result, dramatically simplifying how multi-tool workflows get built.

This uniform shape is also what makes it possible to build general-purpose agent frameworks at all, a framework author can write one planning loop that works with any number of MCP servers, rather than needing bespoke coordination logic for every possible combination of tools.

Without this uniformity, adding an eleventh tool to an agent that already juggles ten others would risk destabilizing the whole system, with it, adding a new tool is simply one more discoverable option the agent can choose to use.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: The complexity of coordinating tools grows with how many exist and how differently each behaves, MCP directly attacks the second half of that equation, even as the first half, the sheer number of tools, keeps growing.

blocks.text: 10. The Versioning and Compatibility Problem

Tools change over time, a new parameter gets added, an old one gets removed. Without a shared protocol, every application connected to a changing tool had to somehow learn about that change and adapt, often only after something silently broke. MCP includes protocol versioning and capability negotiation, covered later in this curriculum, so a client and server can agree, right at connection time, on exactly which version of which features they will use together.

code.content:
# a rough sketch of capability negotiation at connection time
server_capabilities = server.get_capabilities()
if "resources" in server_capabilities and client_supports("resources"):
    enable_resource_features()

blocks.text: Without this negotiation step, a client built against an older version of a server might send a request the server no longer understands, or vice versa, capability negotiation catches this mismatch immediately, at connection time, rather than mid-task.
11. A Single Example Touching Several Problems at Once
" Discovery: the client finds a news-search tool and an email tool. Schema consistency: both tools describe their inputs the same structured way, so the client can call either one with the same code.
Context sharing: the search results become context fed straight into the model’s reasoning.
Error handling: if the email tool fails because an address is invalid, the model gets a clear, standard error it can react to, perhaps by asking the user to confirm their email address.

code.content:
articles = news_client.call_tool("search_news", {"topic": "renewable energy", "days": 7})
summary = model.summarize(articles)
result = email_client.call_tool("send_email", {"to": user_email, "body": summary})
if result.get("error"):
    print("Could not send email:", result["error"]["message"])

blocks.text: Notice that this single example already touches at least five of the ten problems listed earlier, discovery, schema consistency, context sharing, error handling, and multi-tool coordination, which is exactly the point, real tasks rarely involve just one of these problems in isolation.
12. The Testing and Reliability Problem

Testing a custom, one-off tool integration usually meant writing a custom, one-off test harness too, since the shape of the integration itself was unique. With every MCP server following the same discover-call-respond pattern, a single generic test approach, call list_tools, call each tool with valid and invalid arguments, check the response shape, can be reused across every server a team builds, dramatically lowering the cost of testing tool integrations thoroughly.

code.content:
# a generic test pattern that works against any MCP server
for tool in client.list_tools():
    response = client.call_tool(tool["name"], {})   # deliberately missing required args
    assert "error" in response, f"{tool['name']} should reject invalid input"

blocks.text: Some teams go further and build a small internal library of these generic MCP test patterns, reusing the exact same suite of checks against every new server the team builds, catching an entire class of common mistakes automatically before a server ever reaches production.
13. The Onboarding and Documentation Problem

A new engineer joining a team with ten custom, differently-shaped tool integrations has to learn ten different things before they can confidently work on any of them. A new engineer joining a team using MCP servers only has to learn the protocol once, after that, understanding any specific server is mostly a matter of reading its particular tool list, not relearning an entirely different integration pattern from scratch.
This lower onboarding cost compounds over time, as a team grows and as more servers get built, the value of everyone already speaking the same protocol only increases.

blocks.title: A practical benefit
blocks.content: Teams report that writing internal documentation for an MCP server is also simpler, since so much of "how to use this" is already implied by the protocol itself, the server-specific docs only need to cover what is unique to that particular server.

blocks.text: This is one of the quieter, less discussed benefits of adopting a shared protocol, but teams that have gone through both worlds, custom integrations and then MCP servers, consistently mention it as one of the most noticeable day-to-day improvements.
14. Why Solving These Together Matters More Than Solving Them Separately
It would be technically possible to solve any one of these ten problems in isolation, inside a single application, with a bespoke solution.

What makes MCP valuable is solving all of them together, in one shared specification, so that a solution built for problem one, discovery, automatically composes cleanly with the solution for problem six, error handling, because both were designed as part of the same coherent system from the start, rather than bolted together after the fact.

This is analogous to how a well-designed programming language solves memory management, type checking, and error propagation together, as one coherent system, rather than as separate bolt-on libraries that each work slightly differently and occasionally conflict with one another.

It also explains why partial, incomplete implementations of the protocol tend to cause more confusion than skipping it entirely, half of a coherent system is often harder to reason about than none of it.
15. Common Mistakes When Reasoning About These Problems

items: Treating these as ten unrelated feature requests rather than recognizing they all stem from the same root cause, the lack of a shared interface between AI models and the outside world.

Assuming MCP fully solves the security boundary problem on its own, it provides shared vocabulary and mechanisms, the actual safeguards still need to be configured deliberately by whoever runs a server.
Underestimating the versioning and compatibility problem specifically, it tends to matter little on day one and a great deal once a server or client has been running in production for months.
Forgetting that these problems compound, a system with weak discovery and weak error handling fails in ways that are far harder to debug than either weakness alone would cause.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is assuming all ten problems are equally urgent for every project, a small internal prototype might only really feel the discovery and schema consistency problems at first, while the security boundary and versioning problems become pressing only once the system reaches production and keeps running for months.

A sixth common mistake is assuming these ten problems were solved perfectly on the very first version of the specification, like any standard, MCP continues to evolve, with lessons learned from real-world use feeding back into future protocol versions.
16. Practice: Map a Real Tool to These Problems

Pick any tool integration you have seen or built, for a calendar, a database, or a search engine, and go through each of the ten problems above, one at a time, asking how that specific integration handled it, and whether it handled it consistently with any other integration you have seen.

code.content:
problems = ["discovery", "schema consistency", "portability", "context sharing",
            "reusable instructions", "error handling", "session and state",
            "security boundary", "multi-tool coordination", "versioning"]
for prob in problems:
    print(prob, "-> how did this specific integration handle it?")

blocks.text: Once you have gone through this mapping exercise for one integration, try repeating it for a second, very different one, a payment system instead of a calendar, and notice how the same ten problems reappear in a completely different domain, which is exactly why a single shared protocol generalizes so well.

Keep whatever gaps you find from this exercise in mind as you move into the rest of this curriculum, they are a preview of exactly which specific MCP feature, covered in a later module, was designed to close that particular gap.
Key Takeaway

MCP is not solving one abstract inconvenience, it is solving ten separate, concrete technical problems, discovery, schema consistency, portability, context sharing, reusable instructions, error handling, session state, security boundaries, multi-tool coordination, and versioning, all at once, by giving every AI application and every tool the same shared, well-specified interface to build against.

With the motivation and the problem list now both covered, the next lesson turns to MCP Architecture, the actual structural design, host, client, and server, and how requests and responses actually flow between them, that makes solving all ten of these problems possible in practice.

Keep this list of ten problems as a reference point going forward, nearly every remaining module in this curriculum, architecture, communication protocol, resources, tools, prompts, security, is really just a detailed explanation of exactly how MCP solves one or more of these specific problems.
